lead: The World Wide Web is a set of documents named by URLs and fetched on demand. The protocol that fetches them is HTTP, the HyperText Transfer Protocol. A browser sends a short request written in plain text; the server answers with a status line, a few headers and the object itself. That is the whole idea, and it is why you can debug a web server from a terminal. HTTP runs on top of TCP, so bytes arrive in order and none are lost. It is stateless: each request is answered with no memory of the ones before.
prereq: You need: socket programming and DNS from earlier in this unit, and the TCP connection from Unit 5.

blocks.text: A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) names one object on the web. Take https://www.example.com:443/books/net.html?page=2. Read it left to right: https is the scheme, www.example.com is the host, 443 is the port, /books/net.html is the path, and page=2 is the query.

items: The scheme picks the protocol and its default port: 80 for http, 443 for https.
The host is a name; DNS turns it into an IP address before anything else can happen.
The port is left out of the URL when it is the default, which is the usual case.
The path names a file or a program on that server; the query is data handed to that program.

blocks.text: An HTTP message is text with three parts: a start line, header lines, and an optional body after a blank line. That blank line is the separator. Miss it and the receiver treats the headers as body.

blocks.code:
GET /books/net.html HTTP/1.1 Host: www.example.com HTTP/1.1 200 OK Content-Type: text/html Content-Length: 5120

Networks

blocks.text: The request start line is method, path and version: GET /books/net.html HTTP/1.1. The reply start line is version, status code and reason: HTTP/1.1 200 OK. The path in a request to a server holds only the part after the host, never the full URL.
Content-Length states the body size in bytes. Without it, or a chunked encoding, the receiver cannot tell where one message ends and the next begins on a reused connection.
The method is the verb. It says what to do with the named resource.

items: GET asks for the object and must not change anything on the server.
HEAD asks for the headers only, with no body; use it to check size or freshness.
POST sends data in the body, typically a form, and the server decides what to do with it.
PUT stores the body at the URL, replacing what is already there.
DELETE removes the resource at the URL.

blocks.text: The status code is three digits. The first digit gives the class: 1xx information, 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, 5xx server error. Only the common ones matter for an exam.

blocks.text: Headers carry the metadata the body cannot. Host names the site, which is how one IP address serves many sites. Content-Type tells the browser how to read the body, for example text/html or image/png. Content-Length gives its size in bytes. Connection: keep-alive or close decides what happens to the TCP connection next. Cookie carries a small identifier the server handed out earlier.
HTTP/1.0 opened a fresh TCP connection for each object and closed it afterwards. Every object therefore paid for the TCP three-way handshake on top of its own request and reply.
Persistent connections (keep-alive, the default in HTTP/1.1) leave the TCP connection open and send the next request on it. The handshake is now paid once per page instead of once per object.
Pipelining goes further: the client sends several requests back to back without waiting for the replies, and the server answers them in order. On a slow link this removes several round trips.

A proxy cache is a server on your side of the link that keeps copies of objects. Before reusing a stored copy it asks the origin server with a conditional GET carrying If-Modified-Since or If-None-Match. If the object has not changed, the origin replies 304 Not Modified with no body, and the proxy sends its stored copy. One short round trip replaces the whole object.

HTTP is stateless: the server does not remember your previous request. Cookies fix that. The server sends Set-Cookie: id=a7f3 in a reply. The browser stores it for that host and sends Cookie: id=a7f3 in every later request to that host. The state lives in the browser and in the server's table, not in the protocol. Login sessions, shopping carts and "welcome back, Ravi" all work this way.

HTTPS is HTTP carried inside TLS, so the same messages travel encrypted; the handshake and certificates belong to chapter 6.7. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 change the wire format to multiplex many requests over one connection; only a few universities teach them.

examples.question: A web page is one base HTML file plus 3 images. The round-trip time between client and server is 100 ms and transmission time is negligible. Find the time to load the whole page when (a) HTTP/1.0 non-persistent connections are used with no parallel connections, (b) HTTP/1.1 persistent connections with pipelining are used.
steps: Count the objects: 1 base file + 3 images = 4 objects.
Non-persistent: each object needs its own TCP connection. One RTT opens the connection (three-way handshake) and one more RTT carries the request and brings the reply. So 2 RTT per object.
Persistent with pipelining: one TCP connection, so the handshake costs 1 RTT.
The base file costs 1 RTT for request and reply.
The three images are requested back to back without waiting, so all three replies arrive in 1 more RTT.
examples.answer: The page loads in 800 ms with non-persistent HTTP and in 300 ms with persistent HTTP and pipelining.
examples.check:
rtt = 100
objects = 1 + 3
nonpersistent = objects * 2 * rtt
persistent = 3 * rtt
print(nonpersistent)
print(persistent)

traps: Forgetting the TCP setup round trip in the non-persistent case. Each object costs two round trips, not one, because the handshake comes before the request.
Counting one round trip per image when pipelining is allowed. Pipelined requests share a single round trip, so all three images finish together.
Calling HTTP stateful because a site greets you by name. The cookie carries the state; the protocol itself remembers nothing.
Swapping 403 and 404. 403 means the server found the resource and refuses to give it; 404 means there is nothing at that URL. 400 is a malformed request, not a missing page.
Writing the full URL in the request line. A request to a server carries only the path; the host goes into the Host header.

quiz.q: What does it mean to say HTTP is stateless?
quiz.a: The server keeps no memory of earlier requests. Each request is answered on its own, and any continuity must be supplied by cookies or by the application.

quiz.q: List the five parts of a URL and give the default port for http and https.
quiz.a: Scheme, host, port, path, query. Default ports are 80 for http and 443 for https.

quiz.q: Why does a persistent connection load a page faster than a non-persistent one?
quiz.a: The TCP three-way handshake is done once instead of once per object, so each extra object saves one round trip. Pipelining saves more by sending several requests before any reply arrives.

quiz.q: A page has one base HTML file and 4 images. Round-trip time is 50 ms and transmission time is ignored. Find the load time for (a) non-persistent HTTP with no parallel connections, (b) persistent HTTP with pipelining.
quiz.a: 5 objects. (a) Each object costs 2 RTT, so 5 × 2 = 10 RTT = 10 × 50 ms = 500 ms. (b) 1 RTT for TCP setup, 1 RTT for the base file, 1 RTT for all four images = 3 RTT = 150 ms.

quiz.q: A browser shows a stale copy of a page. Which request header and which status code are involved, and why does this save bandwidth?
quiz.a: The client or proxy sends a conditional GET with If-Modified-Since or If-None-Match. If nothing changed, the server answers 304 Not Modified with an empty body, so only a few header bytes cross the network instead of the whole object.

quiz.q: A site shows your name on every page after you log in. Explain why this does not make HTTP a stateful protocol.
quiz.a: On login the server sends Set-Cookie with an identifier. The browser stores it and returns it in the Cookie header of each later request. The server looks the identifier up in its own table. The state sits in the browser and the server, while the protocol still treats each request as independent.

quiz.q: What is the difference between HEAD and GET, and between 301 and 304?
quiz.a: HEAD returns the same headers as GET but no body, so it is used to check size or freshness. 301 says the resource has permanently moved and gives the new URL in Location; 304 says the client's cached copy is still valid and no body follows.

beyond: Not for the exam. Most real traffic is now HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 running over TLS, and browsers multiplex many requests onto one connection per origin, which makes the old per-object round-trip maths a starting point rather than the truth. Content delivery networks place proxy caches close to users and lean on the same conditional GET you saw here, plus Cache-Control headers that set freshness lifetimes. Server push and header compression were the big HTTP/2 ideas, and QUIC replaced TCP underneath HTTP/3. Search next for HTTP/2 frames, HPACK header compression, Cache-Control max-age, and QUIC.
